title: Preventing Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
summary: Every fuel-burning engine makes carbon monoxide, an invisible gas with no smell that builds up fast in enclosed spaces. This talk covers keeping engines out, monitoring, and reacting to symptoms.
talking_points: Never run a gas, diesel, or propane engine - generator, mixer, trowel, pressure washer, or forklift - indoors or in a garage, crawl space, or basement.
Before work, find every possible source of carbon monoxide on the site.
Use electric tools, or keep the engine outside and away from air intakes.
Wear a carbon monoxide monitor when exposure risk is high. Your employer should provide one. It alarms when levels get unsafe.
Know the warning signs: headache, faintness, dizziness, confusion, nausea, and irregular heartbeat.
If you or a coworker shows signs, shut off the equipment, get outside, and call 911.
site_hazards_to_check: Fuel-powered engines running inside enclosed or partly enclosed areas
Poor or no ventilation where engines are operating
Engine exhaust near building air intakes, doors, or windows
No carbon monoxide monitor where several engines run
Workers showing headache, dizziness, or nausea
discussion_questions: What equipment on this site gives off carbon monoxide, and where is it running?
How is this enclosed area being ventilated, and is it enough?
What are the early warning signs, and what do we do if someone feels them?

flags: OSHA mapping verified accurate: 29 CFR 1926.55 (gases, vapors, fumes, dusts, and mists) is the correct construction authority for the CO exposure limit (Appendix A lists CO). Content - never run fuel-burning engines in enclosed/partly enclosed areas, substitute electric tools, keep engines outside and away from air intakes, use a CO monitor/alarm where risk is high, recognize symptoms, evacuate and call 911 - is accurate and complete for a 5-minute talk. No tolerance issues.
